mastery_goal.title: Vectors, Net Force, and Equilibrium
mastery_goal.description: Represent forces with vectors, determine net force, and use the equilibrium rule to connect balanced forces with unchanged velocity.

exemplar.prompt: Two force arrows use the same scale. Arrow A points right and is twice as long as Arrow B, which points left. Compare their directions and relative magnitudes.
exemplar.student_html:
Both arrows use the same scale.

Compare the arrows’ directions and relative force magnitudes.
exemplar.answer: A is rightward and about twice the magnitude of B; B is leftward and smaller.
exemplar.solution: Direction comes from the arrowhead; relative magnitude comes from length when the scale is common.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct direction and relative-size interpretation.

exemplar.prompt: Use the scale 1 cm = 10 N. Draw a vector that represents a 30 N force to the left. Label the vector.
exemplar.student_html:
Use the scale 1 cm = 10 N.

Draw and label a vector that represents a 30 N force to the left.
exemplar.answer: A 3 cm arrow pointing left, labeled 30 N (or equivalent force label).
exemplar.solution: 30 N at 10 N/cm corresponds to 3 cm; arrowhead points left.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Direction, scaled length, and label must all be correct.

exemplar.prompt: A diagram labels two forces 20 N and 40 N, but draws both arrows the same length using the same scale. What is wrong, and how should the diagram change?
exemplar.student_html:
A diagram uses one common scale but draws these two labeled vectors the same length:

What is wrong, and how should the diagram change?
exemplar.answer: The 40 N arrow should be twice as long as the 20 N arrow (if the common linear scale is used).
exemplar.solution: Arrow length carries magnitude information.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Identify length mismatch and specify the required relative length.

exemplar.prompt: Two students push the same cart to the right with forces of 35 N and 20 N. What is the horizontal net force from these pushes?
exemplar.student_html:
Two students push the same cart to the right with forces of 35 N and 20 N.

What is the horizontal net force from these pushes? Include magnitude and direction.
exemplar.answer: 55 N right.
exemplar.solution: Same-direction force magnitudes add: 35 + 20 = 55 N.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct magnitude and direction.

families.evidence_job: Determine net force as difference and direction of larger force.

exemplar.prompt: A cart has a 48 N push right and a 31 N push left. Determine the horizontal net force.
exemplar.student_html:
Opposing horizontal forces

Determine the horizontal net force, including direction.
exemplar.answer: 17 N right.
exemplar.solution: Opposing forces subtract: 48 − 31 = 17 N toward the larger force.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct difference and direction.

exemplar.prompt: A cart is pulled 50 N to the right and also pulled left. The horizontal net force is 14 N to the right. How large is the leftward force?
exemplar.student_html:
A cart is pulled 50 N right and also pulled left. The horizontal net force is 14 N right.

How large is the leftward force?
exemplar.answer: 36 N left.
exemplar.solution: 50 − F_left = 14, so F_left = 36 N.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct missing magnitude and direction.

exemplar.prompt: A force diagram shows 30 N left and 50 N right. Which resultant vector is correct?

exemplar.prompt: A student sees 70 N right and 25 N left, then draws a 45 N resultant arrow to the left. Identify what is correct and what is wrong in the student’s result.
exemplar.student_html:
A student sees 70 N right and 25 N left, then draws a 45 N resultant arrow to the left.

Identify what is correct and what is wrong in the result.
exemplar.answer: The 45 N magnitude is correct; the direction is wrong. The resultant is 45 N right.
exemplar.solution: The net vector points toward the larger force.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Recognize correct magnitude and fix direction.

i_cans.exact_text: I can distinguish static equilibrium from dynamic equilibrium.

families.label: Family A
families.name: Static vs. Dynamic Equilibrium
families.family_purpose: Classify equilibrium state from motion description.
families.exact_text: I can distinguish static equilibrium from dynamic equilibrium.
families.evidence_job: Distinguish equilibrium at rest from equilibrium at constant velocity.
invariants: explicit zero net force or balanced-force condition

exemplar.prompt: A hanging sign is motionless. A cart moves east at constant speed in a straight line. If each has zero net force, classify each as static or dynamic equilibrium.
exemplar.student_html:
Assume each object has zero net force.

  1. A hanging sign is motionless.
  2. A cart moves east at constant speed in a straight line.

Classify each as static equilibrium or dynamic equilibrium.
exemplar.answer: Sign = static equilibrium; cart = dynamic equilibrium.
exemplar.solution: Static equilibrium is rest with zero net force; dynamic equilibrium is constant velocity with zero net force.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Both classifications correct.

families.evidence_job: Interpret a short position/velocity description as equilibrium type.

exemplar.prompt: A cart’s velocity is measured once each second: 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0 m/s east. If the forces are balanced, what kind of equilibrium is this and why?
exemplar.student_html:
Time (s)Velocity
02.0 m/s east
12.0 m/s east
22.0 m/s east
32.0 m/s east

If the forces are balanced, what kind of equilibrium is this? Explain.
exemplar.answer: Dynamic equilibrium because the cart has constant nonzero velocity while net force is zero.
exemplar.solution: The motion is unchanged but not at rest.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Identify dynamic equilibrium and cite constant velocity.

families.label: Family C
families.name: Equilibrium Does Not Mean Rest

families.exact_text: I can distinguish static equilibrium from dynamic equilibrium.
families.evidence_job: Explain dynamic equilibrium.
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A student says, “If an object is in equilibrium, it must be stopped.” Explain why this is incomplete and give a valid moving example.
exemplar.student_html:
A student says:

“If an object is in equilibrium, it must be stopped.”

Explain why this is incomplete and give a valid moving example of equilibrium.
exemplar.answer: An object can be in dynamic equilibrium while moving at constant velocity in a straight line; e.g., a cart moving steadily with balanced forces.
exemplar.solution: Equilibrium means zero net force, which permits either rest or constant velocity.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: State dynamic equilibrium and a physically valid example.

i_cans.exact_text: I can explain how an object can have forces acting on it and still have zero net force.

families.label: Family A
families.name: Balanced Forces Still Exist
families.family_purpose: Explain zero net force with individual forces present.
families.exact_text: I can explain how an object can have forces acting on it and still have zero net force.
families.evidence_job: Connect equal opposing forces to zero vector sum.
invariants: at least two real forces balance
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A 25 N book rests on a table and the table pushes upward with 25 N. Explain how forces can be acting while the net force is zero.
exemplar.student_html:
Forces on the resting book

Explain how forces can be acting while the net force is zero.
exemplar.answer: The 25 N upward support and 25 N downward weight are equal and opposite, so their vector sum is zero.
exemplar.solution: Individual forces need not be zero for the net force to be zero.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Identify both forces and explain cancellation.

families.label: Family B
families.name: Multiple Forces, Zero Sum

families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A box has two rightward pushes of 10 N and 15 N and one leftward pull of 25 N. What is the horizontal net force? Explain why the box can still have forces acting on it.
exemplar.student_html:
A box has two rightward pushes of 10 N and 15 N, and one leftward pull of 25 N.

What is the horizontal net force? Explain why the box can still have forces acting on it.
exemplar.answer: 0 N; 10 + 15 = 25, so the forces cancel even though three forces act.
exemplar.solution: Net force is the vector sum of all forces.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct sum and explanation of nonzero individual forces.

families.label: Family C
families.name: No Motion Does Not Mean No Forces

families.evidence_job: Use equilibrium to correct a force-presence misconception.
invariants: stationary object has a clear support interaction

exemplar.prompt: A student says, “The hanging plant is not moving, so no forces are acting on it.” Explain the error and name two forces that can act while the plant remains in equilibrium.
exemplar.student_html:
A student says:

“The hanging plant is not moving, so no forces are acting on it.”

Explain the error and name two forces that can act while the plant remains in equilibrium.
exemplar.answer: Weight downward and support/tension upward can balance, giving zero net force while both forces act.
exemplar.solution: Rest supports zero net force, not necessarily absence of forces.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Name valid opposing forces and explain balance.

exemplar.scoring_guidance: 65 N left and link to zero net force.

exemplar.prompt: A box is in equilibrium. Vertically, support and weight are already equal. Horizontally, 18 N acts left and an unknown force acts right. Determine the unknown force and explain why the vertical forces do not change this horizontal answer.
exemplar.student_html:
A box is in equilibrium. Vertically, support and weight are already equal. Horizontally, 18 N left and an unknown force act.

Determine the unknown horizontal force. Explain why the already-balanced vertical forces do not change this horizontal answer.
exemplar.answer: 18 N right; the vertical forces cancel in the vertical direction, while horizontal equilibrium requires the horizontal forces to cancel.
exemplar.solution: Equilibrium is satisfied independently in perpendicular directions in this simple model.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Correct force and axis reasoning.

families.family_purpose: Connect zero net force to unchanged velocity.
families.exact_text: I can explain why zero net force means an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line.

exemplar.prompt: A cart is moving west at 3 m/s. The net force on it becomes zero and remains zero. Describe its motion afterward.
exemplar.student_html:
A cart is moving west at 3 m/s. The net force on it becomes zero and remains zero.

Describe its motion afterward.
exemplar.answer: It continues west at 3 m/s in a straight line (constant velocity).
exemplar.solution: Zero net force means no change in velocity.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: State unchanged speed and direction.

families.name: Match Force State to Motion State

families.exact_text: I can explain why zero net force means an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line.
families.student_action: Select all descriptions consistent with zero net force.
families.evidence_job: Recognize the motion states compatible with zero net force.
invariants: include rest, constant straight-line velocity, and velocity-changing distractors

exemplar.prompt: Which of these can occur while net force is zero: (1) resting on a table, (2) moving north at constant velocity, (3) speeding up east, (4) moving in a circle at constant speed? Explain your choices.
exemplar.student_html:
Which situations can occur while the net force is zero?

  1. resting on a table
  2. moving north at constant velocity
  3. speeding up east
  4. moving in a circle at constant speed

Explain your choices.
exemplar.answer: 1 and 2 only. Speeding up changes velocity; circular motion changes direction, so both require nonzero net force.
exemplar.solution: Zero net force permits only unchanged velocity, including zero velocity.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Choose 1 and 2 and explain why 3/4 involve velocity change.

families.label: Family C
families.name: Zero Net Force Does Not Make an Object Stop
families.family_purpose: Correct the stop-at-zero-net-force misconception.
families.exact_text: I can explain why zero net force means an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line.
families.evidence_job: Explain persistence of motion under zero net force.
invariants: misconception equates zero net force with zero velocity
forbidden_variations: change only names/nouns while preserving the same finished prompt
families.fresh_instance_rule: Preserve the evidence job and invariants; vary only declared axes. A fresh instance must not be a noun-only or number-only clone when conceptual reasoning is the evidence target.

exemplar.prompt: A student predicts that when the net force on a moving cart becomes zero, the cart must immediately stop. Explain the mistake.
exemplar.student_html:
A student predicts:

“When the net force on a moving cart becomes zero, the cart must immediately stop.”

Explain the mistake using Newton’s First Law.
exemplar.answer: Zero net force means velocity stays unchanged; if already moving, it continues at constant velocity rather than stopping immediately.
exemplar.solution: Stopping is itself a change in velocity and would require nonzero net force during the slowdown.
exemplar.scoring_guidance: Explain unchanged velocity and why stopping would be a change.
